title: DDWS Organised Regional Review Meeting of States/UTs under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 at IIM Bangalore
subtitle: Secretary, DDWS urges States to strengthen source sustainability, water quality surveillance and service delivery under JJM 2.0
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 7:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, organised a regional review meeting of States and Union Territories under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 at the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore (IIM Bangalore) today. The meeting was chaired by Shri Ashok K. K. Meena, Secretary, DDWS, in the presence of Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, Additional Secretary & Mission Director, National Jal Jeevan Mission (NJJM), and attended by senior officials from States and UTs. The meeting reviewed the progress of JJM 2.0 and discussed key reform measures relating to source sustainability, water quality surveillance, digital governance, community participation and long-term sustainability of rural water supply systems.
In his opening address,
Shri Ashok K. K. Meena
emphasised that Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 marks a significant shift from infrastructure creation to sustainable and accountable service delivery. He urged States and UTs to accelerate implementation of approved schemes and effectively utilise available resources while ensuring that investments are directed towards fully functional schemes delivering reliable drinking water services to rural households. Stressing the importance of outcomes-based implementation, he underlined that expenditure must be translated into functional infrastructure supported by complete source-to-household connectivity, robust digital records and effective monitoring systems.
Secretary Shri Meena highlighted that Jal Jeevan Mission has transformed rural drinking water access across the country, with more than 15.96 crore rural households now having tap water connections compared to only 3.27 crore households at the time of the Mission's launch in August 2019. He noted that the focus of JJM 2.0 is on sustaining these gains through source sustainability, financial and operational efficiency, water quality assurance and citizen-centric service delivery.
Shri Meena called upon States to expedite implementation of both single-village and multi-village water supply schemes, particularly in quality-affected areas, and ensure timely utilisation of available resources.
Referring to the decisions taken during recent sectoral deliberations on water governance, he urged States and UTs to establish effective mechanisms for monitoring and implementing agreed reform measures to further strengthen service delivery under JJM 2.0.
Highlighting findings emerging from
Jal Seva Adhayan
, he observed that pipeline leakages and breakages continue to be the leading cause of water supply disruptions, followed by power cuts and low-voltage related challenges. He emphasised the need for States to adopt both immediate and long-term solutions to improve the reliability of rural water supply systems and ensure uninterrupted drinking water services to rural households.
The Secretary further underscored the importance of exploring renewable energy solutions for rural drinking water infrastructure. He informed that discussions are underway with the
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) to examine the solarisation of drinking water assets across the country.
He noted that
innovative approaches leveraging solar energy can reduce operational costs, improve service reliability and strengthen the long-term sustainability of rural drinking water systems.
Addressing the participants,
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM
, highlighted the importance of addressing operational challenges affecting rural water supply schemes. Referring to findings emerging from Jal Seva Adhayan and related assessments, he noted that low voltage and poor power quality continue to impact service delivery in several areas. He emphasised that
reducing power-related costs can significantly improve operational sustainability and urged States and UTs to work collectively towards identifying practical solutions
for improving energy efficiency and reducing recurring operation and maintenance expenditure.
Prof. Gopal Naik, JJM Professor Chair, IIM Bangalore
, presented a study titled
“Power Cost Optimization in JJM Scheme”
. The study examined various energy configurations for rural water supply systems, including grid-based and solar-powered models, and assessed their implications on operational and life-cycle costs. The presentation highlighted opportunities for reducing recurring operation and maintenance expenditure, improving affordability of water services and enhancing the financial sustainability of rural water supply schemes through innovative energy solutions.
The programme also featured presentations on research related to drinking water quality monitoring and management using Water Quality Management Information System (WQMIS) data. The findings indicated significant improvements in drinking water quality compliance across several parameters following implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission and highlighted opportunities for strengthening laboratory ecosystems, independent surveillance mechanisms and community-led water quality management.
During the discussions, Secretary, DDWS emphasised the importance of establishing independent water quality surveillance mechanisms to strengthen transparency and accountability in rural water supply systems. He underscored the need to make water quality information available to Gram Panchayats and communities and highlighted the role of Gram Sabhas in reviewing water quality findings and identifying remedial measures. He noted that community participation and data-driven decision-making will be critical for improving long-term service delivery outcomes under JJM 2.0.
During the review meeting, States and UTs also discussed progress on key JJM 2.0 priorities, including State Implementation Plans, financial reconciliation, Har Ghar Jal certification in PM-JANMAN villages, Jal Arpan, digital governance initiatives and water quality management. The meeting concluded with States and UTs sharing progress, challenges and best practices and reaffirming their commitment to advancing the Mission's vision of sustainable water security through cooperative federalism, technology-enabled governance and Jan Bhagidari.
In his
concluding remarks, Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM
urged State/UTs to accelerate implementation of key reform initiatives under JJM 2.0. Referring to Jal Arpan, the formal handing over of schemes to GP and VWSC he emphasised the need to complete in all Har Ghar Jal villages and ensure generation of certificates in the approved regional languages.
Shri Soan further called upon State/UTs to expedite water quality testing, particularly in Anganwadi Centres and other public institutions and ensure timely uploading of test results on the designated digital platforms. He urged to operationalise the O&M Manual at the Gram Panchayat level, actively utilise the Decision Support System (DSS) for source sustainability planning and monitoring, and strengthen coordination with Panchayati Raj Institutions for effective management of rural water supply systems. He also emphasised timely submission of inputs on DSS, completion of capacity-building activities, adherence to Finance Commission compliance requirements and preparation of clear implementation plans for achieving JJM 2.0 reform milestones.

title: Hindi Promotion Should Be Through Creating Opportunities and Stake, Not by Imposition: Dr. Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
Official Hindi Should Be Simple, Easy to Understand and Closer to Everyday Usage: Union Minister

Technology and AI Have Significantly Improved the Quality of Hindi Translation in Government Work: Dr. Jitendra Singh

Hindi Usage Has Increased Significantly Over the Last 10–12 Years after PM Sh Narendra Modi took over; Southern Officers Also Using Hindi Extensively: Dr. Jitendra Singh

DoPT Will Seriously Consider Suggestions of Hindi Advisory Committee and Refer Matters Beyond Its Mandate to Concerned Ministries
ministry: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 3:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology, Earth Sciences and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh today emphasised that promotion of Hindi should be based on creating greater opportunities and stake in the language rather than making its use appear imposed. Addressing the third meeting of the Hindi Advisory Committee of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, he said greater use of Hindi would naturally follow when knowledge of the language creates opportunities for employment and professional growth. The
Kaushal Patrika of the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT)
was also launched on the occasion.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the suggestions received from members of the Hindi Advisory Committee had been noted and that the Department would make serious efforts towards their implementation. He said suggestions falling outside the jurisdiction of the Department would be forwarded to the concerned Ministries and Departments so that they could be examined at the appropriate level.
Referring to a suggestion regarding language options in competitions conducted by the Ministry of Skill Development, the Minister said that such options could help make these initiatives more accessible to beneficiaries from smaller towns, cities and rural areas. He suggested that language options, including suitable oral components where appropriate, could make such initiatives more accessible, and said the suggestion could be conveyed to the Ministry concerned.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also referred to the suggestion of involving Hindi Advisory Committee members in programmes for teaching Hindi in schools. He said such proposals could be taken up with the Ministry of Education, particularly where programmes involve teachers and educational institutions, as the Personnel Department by itself may not be in a position to undertake such activities.
The Minister stressed that while a substantial amount of work in the Department is already carried out in Hindi, it may not always be practical to insist on 100 per cent use of Hindi, particularly in official communication with non-Hindi-speaking States. He said the sensitivities and convenience of people and officials in different linguistic regions have to be kept in mind.
Emphasising the need for simple and accessible official Hindi, Dr. Jitendra Singh said that government communication should not use unnecessarily difficult or highly formal Hindi. He said language used in official work should be such that it can be easily understood in everyday communication, rather than appearing like a literal translation from English.
The Minister said there has been a significant change in the use of Hindi during the last 10–12 years after PM Shri Narendra Modi took over, including increased use of the language by officers from southern parts of the country. He cited examples of officers and personnel in scientific and technical establishments using Hindi extensively in their official work despite being based in predominantly non-Hindi-speaking regions.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also highlighted improvements in the quality of translation in government work. Referring to the earlier occurrence of incorrect and sometimes misleading translations, he said such problems have reduced considerably. He noted that technology and AI-driven systems, along with the availability of larger datasets, are now contributing to improvements in translation, including in technically sensitive areas.
The Minister, however, cautioned against viewing Hindi usage in isolation from the wider requirement of knowledge and professional competence. He said that insisting exclusively on Hindi, particularly in specialised fields where adequate literature and terminology may not be readily available, should not become a barrier to knowledge acquisition. He referred to the experience of introducing Hindi in medical education and stressed that original technical terms can continue to be retained where necessary, while explanations and teaching can be provided in Hindi.
Dr. Jitendra Singh reiterated that creating a stake in a language is more effective for its promotion than merely imposing its use. He said that as Hindi becomes increasingly useful for employment and professional opportunities, people would have a natural incentive to learn and use it. He referred to the growing demand for Hindi learning even in regions where it was traditionally less prevalent, linking such interest to emerging employment opportunities.
The Minister said the Hindi Advisory Committee has an important role in providing informed suggestions and guidance to the Department. He invited members to continue sharing their ideas and suggestions in writing or through other appropriate means, adding that the Department would continue to work towards improvements based on their guidance.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the larger objective should be to promote Hindi in a manner that is simple, natural and inclusive, so that its use does not create a sense of imposition. He emphasised that the ultimate goal is to expand the use and reach of Hindi while ensuring that it remains aligned with the country’s linguistic diversity and everyday communication needs.
The meeting also provided an opportunity for members of the Hindi Advisory Committee to place their suggestions before the Department on matters relating to the promotion and wider use of Hindi in official work.

title: CM of Assam, Dr. Himanta Biswa Sarma to inaugurate Second Regional Workshop for North-Eastern States under Sādhana Śrinkhla (Series) 2026
subtitle:
Capacity Building Commission to organise workshop at Guwahati on 9th October 2026 to focus on Training Institutes Transformation

Strengthening Adaptive Development and Humane Aptitude for National Advancement
ministry: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 12:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The second regional workshop of Sādhana Śrinkhla (Series) 2026, being organised by the Capacity Building Commission (CBC), will be held at Guwahati, Assam, on 9 October 2026. The workshop will be inaugurated by the
Hon’ble Chief Minister of Assam, Dr. Himanta Biswa Sarma
, and will bring together stakeholders from all eight States of the North Eastern region, namely Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. Heads and faculty of Government Training Institutes, subject matter experts, industry partners and other stakeholders will also participate in the deliberations.
Sādhana Śrinkhla (Series) 2026 is a nationwide series of four regional workshops being organised by the Capacity Building Commission to advance the transformation of Civil Service Training Institutions into Capacity Building Institutions under National Program for Civil Services Capacity Building. Following the inaugural workshop held at Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh, on 29–30 September 2026, the Guwahati workshop will be the second workshop in the series.
The workshop will provide a platform for participating States and Training Institutes to share their experiences, deliberate on opportunities and challenges in institutional transformation, and identify practical measures for strengthening their capacity-building ecosystems. Particular emphasis will be placed on translating the proposed reforms into State-specific action plans, including measures to improve institutional governance, strengthen faculty capabilities, and enable Training Institutes to become digitally empowered and future-ready.
From National Consultation to Regional Action
Training Institutes form the bedrock of a future-ready, responsive and citizen-centric civil service and have a critical role in realising the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Over the past year, the Commission has undertaken an extensive consultative journey, including Regional Task Force meetings, Sādhana Saptah held from 2 to 8 April 2026, and the National Departmental Summit on Institutionalising Capacity Building in May 2026.
These consultations underscored the need for a unified framework to guide Training Institutes in their evolution from standalone training providers into strategic, competency-driven capacity building institutions. Building on this momentum, Sādhana Śrinkhla (Series) seeks to take the national dialogue on institutional reform to the regions, engaging States and Training Institutes in contextualising the proposed reforms and translating them into actionable priorities.
Towards a Training Institute Transformation Framework
Through the regional workshops, the Commission is engaging with State Governments, Training Institutes and other stakeholders to develop a comprehensive Training Institute Transformation Framework that responds to the diverse needs and institutional realities across the country.
The consultations focus on strengthening institutional governance and leadership, improving operational effectiveness and collaboration, building faculty and institutional competencies, and enabling digital transformation and the adoption of emerging technologies, including Artificial Intelligence. A central objective is to enable Training Institutes to move from largely supply-driven training to demand-responsive, role- and competency-based capacity building.

title: New metal-free porous material can help produce affordable clean energy
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 3:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A breakthrough metal-free catalyst developed by scientists could significantly reduce the cost of next-generation clean-energy technologies.
In energy storage devices such as zinc–air (Zn–air) batteries, oxygen from the air reacts with the electrode in a process known as the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). The efficiency with which the battery operates is determined by this reaction. Zn–air batteries are a promising option for next-generation energy storage as they utilise the abundant, inexpensive and relatively safe element zinc while drawing oxygen directly from the air, thus eliminating the need to store an active cathode material. Compared with conventional lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries, Zn–air batteries offer the potential for higher theoretical energy density, lower material cost, improved safety and greater sustainability. However, challenges related to rechargeability, cycle life and ORR kinetics remain.
Compared with hydrogen fuel cells, Zn–air batteries can provide a simpler, more compact energy storage solution that does not require high-pressure hydrogen storage or extensive hydrogen infrastructure. However, both Zn–air batteries and hydrogen fuel cells critically rely on efficient oxygen electrochemistry. Currently, many clean-energy technologies, particularly hydrogen fuel cells, depend on platinum, one of the world’s rarest and most expensive metals, as an efficient ORR catalyst. While platinum provides excellent catalytic performance, its high cost, scarcity and limited availability remain major barriers to large-scale deployment. Therefore, developing efficient, platinum-free ORR catalysts is crucial for realising the cost, sustainability and scalability advantages of Zn–air batteries, and for advancing affordable clean-energy technologies.
A team of researchers from S. N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences (SNBNCBS), Kolkata, and Institute of Nano Science and Technology (INST), Mohali, both institute of Department of Science and Technology (DST) as well as from SRM University, Amaravati, has now demonstrated that a specially designed metal-free organic porous material, prepared from 2,4,6-tris(4-aminophenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (TTT) and  4,8-dioxo-4,8-dihydrobenzo[1,2-b:4,5-b’]dithiophene-2,6-dicarbaldehyde (DHTD) linkers, named as TTT-DHTD. Interestingly, TTT-DHTD can perform almost as well as platinum without using any precious metals when used as the air-electrode catalyst in Zn–air batteries. This was published in the journal Science Advances.
Built entirely from abundant elements such as carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, and hydrogen, the material forms an ultra-porous, honeycomb-like network that efficiently converts oxygen into electricity—a key step in generating power in a fuel cell. Laboratory tests showed that the new catalyst achieved about 96% of the performance of commercial platinum catalysts, while remaining remarkably stable. Even after 120 hours of continuous operation, the material maintained its performance without the degradation or contamination that often affects conventional metal-based catalysts.
The researchers led by Dr. Pradip Pachfule from SNBNCBS, Prof. Ramendra Sundar Dey from INST, and Prof. Ranjit Thapa from SRM University, Amaravati, also used advanced computer simulations to understand why the material performs so well. They found that its carefully engineered molecular structure creates ideal sites where oxygen molecules can readily attach and react, enabling electricity to be generated quickly and efficiently.
Replacing platinum with inexpensive organic materials could dramatically reduce the cost of Zn-air cells, making clean transportation, portable power systems, and renewable energy storage more affordable and accessible. This development also highlights India's growing leadership in sustainable materials research.
Fig 1.
Metal-free covalent organic framework electrocatalyst for efficient oxygen reduction reaction and high-performance Zn–air batteries (Image credit: ChatGPT).
By combining innovative molecular design with advanced computational studies, the researchers have demonstrated that earth-abundant materials can rival the performance of precious metals in one of the most important reactions for clean-energy technologies.
As the world searches for cleaner and more economical energy solutions, breakthroughs like TTT-DHTD bring us one step closer to a future where efficient, durable, and affordable fuel cells become part of everyday life.

title: Sagarmanthan 2026 Opens as India Charts the Course for a Trusted, Rules-Based Global Maritime Order
subtitle:
The Oceans Do Not Separate Us, They Connect Us: PM Narendra Modi's Message Sets the Tone for the Great Oceans Dialogue

Prime Minister Narendra Modi calls for a free, open, secure and rules-based maritime order that brings peace, prosperity and progress for all

Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal presents Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 as India's offer of partnership to the world

Seas of Partnership: India Brings Korea, EU, Australia, Norway, UAE, Bhutan & Africa Together on Day One at Sagarmanthan 2026
ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 9:06PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The 3rd edition of
Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue
, organised by the
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW)
in partnership with the
Observer Research Foundation (ORF)
, opened here today. The Dialogue opened with a message from
Prime Minister Narendra Modi
calling for a free, open, secure and rules-based maritime order. Building on the Prime Minister's vision,
Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal
set out a global maritime order built on trust, shared prosperity and partnership, with India as a guide and anchor for nations navigating profound change.
In his message to the Dialogue, Prime Minister
Shri Narendra Modi
recalled that in Indian tradition the churning of the ocean is associated with the discovery of new possibilities. He traced India's maritime heritage from Lothal to the Cholas and the naval vision of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, and reaffirmed India's vision of a free, open, secure and rules-based maritime order. "The oceans do not separate us, they connect us, because what happens in one part of the world can have an impact far beyond its shores," the Prime Minister said, underlining why dialogue and global cooperation matter more than ever.
The first day of Sagarmanthan brought together ministers from different countries, naval leadership, port authorities, shipbuilders, financiers and multilateral institutions from five continents. Delegations and experts from Australia, Belgium, Bhutan, the European Union, France, Norway, the Republic of Korea, the UAE, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Ghana, Egypt, Seychelles, Ecuador and others joined the OECD, UN Trade and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the African Union in a single conversation on the future of the oceans.
Closing the day's proceedings in a high-level conversation titled Maritime Amrit Kaal 2047: India's Ocean Vision and a New Era of Global Maritime Cooperation, Sonowal described India's maritime transformation under Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047, PM Gati Shakti and the Sagarmala programme as a contribution to the world, not only to India. In conversation with ORF President Dr. Samir Saran, he positioned India as a Vishwaguru on the oceans: a nation that shares its knowledge, capacity and talent to help shape a more collaborative global ocean agenda.
"India's bond with the sea is civilisational. For thousands of years, Indian sailors carried goods, ideas and culture across the oceans as partners, never as conquerors," said
Sarbananda Sonowal
. "Under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India is once again offering the world a maritime model rooted in trust, capability and mutual benefit. That is the spirit of India as Vishwaguru: we lead by example and we grow together with our partners."
"The global maritime order is going through a great churning of disruption, fragmentation and technological change,"
Sonowal
added. "Out of this churning, India is determined to bring forth amrit for the world: resilient supply chains, green shipping corridors, a world-class shipbuilding ecosystem and a skilled seafaring workforce that every nation can rely on. Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 is our roadmap to Viksit Bharat, and an open invitation to partners across every ocean."
Delivering the scene-setting ministerial address at the formal opening of the conference,
Union Minister of State for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Shantanu Thakur
highlighted how India's port-led development and new-generation maritime laws are building capacity for the wider region. Vijay Kumar, Secretary, MoPSW, delivered the opening address, and Dr. Samir Saran, President, ORF, delivered the welcome remarks.
"Ports today are not just gateways for cargo; they are strategic assets that shape competitiveness, energy security and trust between nations," said
Shantanu Thakur
. "With our major ports having nearly doubled their capacity and a modern legal framework now in place, India is ready to serve not only its own growth but the trade of the entire Indo-Pacific and beyond."
The Inaugural Ministerial Plenary, Tides of Trust: Ports, Partnerships, and the Making of a New Maritime Century, moderated by Dr. Samir Saran, examined how ports and shipping networks are being rethought as strategic assets. The panel featured Kevin Rudd, Former Prime Minister of Australia and Global President & CEO, Asia Society; Ms. Annick De Ridder, Flemish Minister of Mobility, Public Works, Ports and Sport, Belgium; Chandra Bahadur Gurung, Minister of Infrastructure and Transport, Bhutan; Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, India; and Rizwan Soomar, CEO and MD, DP World. Earlier, Soomar and Dr. Saran set the tone in The Great Churning: Trade, Power and Opportunity, a conversation on how maritime connectivity is redefining economic power.
India-EU Green Shipping Corridor:
The India-EU Green Shipping Corridor brings together India's potential in green fuel production with emerging European demand, creating new opportunities for green ammonia and methanol trade and maritime decarbonisation. Following the launch of the corridor's pre-feasibility study in 2025 and the establishment of an industry coalition in 2026, the initiative is moving towards implementation. The session, India-EU Green Shipping Corridor: Innovation, Action and Scale, an associated event with the RMI, formally launched the coalition, bringing government and industry together to outline a pathway from feasibility to execution, mobilise investment and partnerships, and build a commercially viable and scalable green shipping corridor. Ministerial addresses were delivered by Apostolos Tzitzikostas, Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism, European Commission, and Shantanu Thakur, with opening remarks by Vijay Kumar.
India-Korea in the Indo-Pacific:
The roundtable discussion, India-Korea in the Indo-Pacific: Maritime Cooperation and Economic Resilience, an associated event with the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP), reviewed progress since the April 2026 India-Republic of Korea Summit, with a focus on the implementation of the India-Korea Comprehensive Framework for Partnership in Shipbuilding, Shipping and Maritime Logistics, and its alignment with the Special Strategic Partnership. It assessed how India and Korea are advancing cooperation across shipbuilding ecosystems, maritime logistics, port-led development, and supply chain integration, with emphasis on structured collaboration between government stakeholders and industry actors, including shipyards, shipping companies, port operators, and maritime technology firms. The discussion placed these developments within an evolving Indo-Pacific maritime and economic architecture shaped by supply chain disruptions, geopolitical fragmentation, and shifting patterns of trade and industry, and explored how the India-Korea partnership can strengthen maritime connectivity, diversify trade links, and deepen industrial collaboration to build more resilient systems in the Indo-Pacific. The session also saw the launch of the edited volume Oceans of Alignment: India-South Korea Cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.
Corridors, measurement and Africa:
Economic corridors are emerging as important platforms for reshaping trade, investment and regional integration. Yet their success depends on more than physical infrastructure. The curtain raiser session, Governing the Corridors of Tomorrow: Lessons for IMEC, examined the governance architecture needed to translate IMEC from strategic vision into a functioning economic corridor. It explored how India, Europe and partner countries can build the frameworks, partnerships and institutional mechanisms needed to support investment, interoperability and long-term momentum, while ensuring that IMEC remains adaptable to a changing geopolitical and economic landscape.
As countries accelerate efforts to develop sustainable blue economies, the ability to measure progress, identify gaps, and align policies with long-term objectives is becoming increasingly important. The OECD Blue Economy Scoreboards offer a comprehensive framework to support evidence-based policymaking by enabling countries to benchmark progress, identify priorities, and strengthen coordination across sectors. The session, Tracking the Transition to Sustainable Blue Economies, an associated event with the OECD, brought together policymakers, international organisations, and experts to discuss how improved measurement frameworks can support more effective blue economy strategies, guide investment decisions, and foster international cooperation towards sustainable and inclusive ocean development.
Africa's maritime corridors are becoming increasingly important to global trade resilience as geopolitical disruptions, chokepoint vulnerabilities, and shifting supply chains reshape the movement of goods and resources. Initiatives such as the Lobito Corridor and growing investments in regional connectivity highlight Africa's potential to diversify trade routes, strengthen supply chain resilience and unlock the blue economy's potential. The session, Africa's Blue Gateways: From Corridors to Engines of Connectivity, explored how Africa can transform its maritime corridors from transit pathways into engines of connectivity, economic growth, and global trade resilience.
Across its sessions, the first day of Sagarmanthan, 2026 carried a single message as trade routes, technologies and alliances are reshaped, India is stepping forward as a trusted builder, partner and guide for the global maritime community. Sagarmanthan 2026 continues with further ministerial and expert sessions.

title: NCSC Intervention Results in Mandatory Reporting of SC Beneficiaries under Key Financial Schemes

Directions Issued to SLBC/UTLBC Convenors Across States and Union Territories; Action-Taken Report to be Submitted by October 9, 2026
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 7:28PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Following the intervention of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC), the Department of Financial Services (DFS), Ministry of Finance, has issued directions for mandatory reporting of assistance provided to Scheduled Caste beneficiaries under major government financial schemes.
Under the directions, State Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs) and UTLBCs have been advised to include scheme-wise and bank-wise details of the number and percentage of Scheduled Caste beneficiaries assisted under the identified schemes in their periodic review meetings.
They have also been directed to regularly share the information with the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and submit an action-taken report to the Department of Financial Services by October 9, 2026, including details regarding data availability and any issues in compilation.
The Department of Financial Services has further directed that the reporting should be undertaken using data already available with banks and implementing agencies. This will ensure consistency in definitions and methodology without creating parallel reporting requirements. SLBCs and UTLBCs have also been asked to furnish an update on the action taken within 30 days.
On September 24, 2026, Secretary, NCSC, Shri Vivek Kumar Dewangan, wrote to the Secretary, Department of Financial Services, highlighting that State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) reports were not reflecting the percentage of Scheduled Caste families and beneficiaries assisted under major government schemes, including Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (PMMY), Stand-Up India, Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), PM SVANidhi, CGTMSE and MSME Business Loans.
The Commission had pointed out that the absence of such data was hindering the discharge of its Constitutional mandate under Article 338(5)(c) to evaluate the progress of socio-economic development of Scheduled Castes. In response, the Department of Financial Services issued directions dated October 5, 2026 to all SLBC/UTLBC Convenors across States and Union Territories.

content:
Introduction:
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has been following
System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)
, endorsed by the United Nations Statistical Commission.
Since 2018, MoSPI has been started working on various aspects of the environment accounts. Given the wide scope of this work, a clear strategic roadmap was needed. Accordingly, NSO, MoSPI released the
‘Strategy for Environmental-Economic Accounts in India 2022–2026’
to guide the development of environmental accounting in India wherein certain areas were identified, such as Material Flow Accounts (MFAs), Ocean Accounts, Energy Accounts, and Thematic Accounts for Biodiversity and Urban Areas to work upon for the said period.
Accordingly, MoSPI has initiated work on various aspects of environmental accounting and has initiated studies, brought out publications and reports covering areas such as forests, biodiversity, wetlands, ocean accounts, soil, water quality, croplands, energy, residuals, urban ecosystems and pollination services.
The Ministry is also undertaken efforts to expand and strengthen the coverage of Environmental Accounts.
About the strategy document 2026-30:
In order to effectively measure and monitor such a vast and evolving domain of environment accounting, to build upon the efforts and advancements made so far, it is essential to establish a forward-looking strategic framework for the further development of Environmental Accounts. The strategy document would delineate key action points and the steps required to progress towards the desired outcomes, address data gaps, advance and expand the coverage of accounts, and identify priority areas and milestones to guide implementation and monitor progress Hence, MoSPI has compiled and released a document titled”
Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India 2026–2030”
.
The current document titled ‘
Strategy for Environmental Economic Accounts in India: 2026-2030
’ is an extension of the earlier document and is intended to provide a broad road-map  with a objective of covering new subjects or enhancement of scope of the subjects like
forest, minerals, soil resources, land, water, carbon stock, Environmental related activities, Biodiversity, environment statistics
etc.  for the development of environmental accounting in India. These areas are mainly selected on the basis of recommendations mentioned in the report of "Green National Account in India A Framework" and the SEEA-CF framework.
The document is comprehensive and elaborative in nature and provides an overview of India’s journey in the field of environmental accounting. It highlights the initiatives undertaken by MoSPI to address existing data gaps, advance the development of environmental-economic accounting, potential data sources, the policy implications and establish a clear action plan for the coming years.
Utility of the Strategy Document for Stakeholders:
The developments under
System of National Accounts 2025
, particularly the recognition of natural resource accounting within the national accounting framework, strengthen the importance of environmental accounting.  Subjects /area covered under this roadmap will provide opportunity to better understand the links between natural resources, the economy and the environment. The Strategic Framework will also help in identifying and addressing data gaps in these areas.
The document is envisaged to serve as a useful reference and guiding framework for individual States and Union Territories that may wish to initiate or strengthen their work in the area of environmental accounting.
This Strategy document is a guidance tool that is self-evolving in nature. Overall, the strategy document provides a direction for the development of environmental accounting in India during the period 2026-30
for strengthening the statistical and accounting ecosystem and for facilitating a more systematic and coordinated approach towards environmental-economic accounting.

title: Additive Manufacturing in India
subtitle: Building India's Future with Next Generation Digital Manufacturing
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 12:05PM by PIB Delhi
content:
India is emerging as a competitive player in digital revolution through Additive Manufacturing (AM), a 3D printing technology in which digital file controls the process of manufacturing. The National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM) is a strategy introduced in 2022 to build India's AM ecosystem. It has made steady progress so far, training over 1,54,000 individuals and supporting 56 AM start-ups. The strategy is now moving into its NSAM 2.0 phase, planning even bigger market than NSAM 1.0 - positioning AM as a building block of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat.
India's Technology Story is Changing Gears
Over the last decade, India has moved from being only a user of technology to becoming a builder of it. Digital public infrastructure has already shown the world how India can build digital systems at population scale. That same confidence is now spreading from the digital world into the physical one - into how India designs, builds and manufactures things. This is where
Additive Manufacturing (AM)
enters the picture. It is the emerging technology and innovation that is quietly turning digital designs into real, physical objects.
Additive Manufacturing is becoming one of the newest engineering frontiers of India's manufacturing journey. The global AM machines market is projected to touch USD 149 billion by 2035, with the AM-electronics supply chain set to grow from USD 18 billion to USD 112 billion. This gives India a real opening to become a competitive manufacturer of AM platforms across polymers, metals, composites, ceramics and semiconductor-grade materials.
Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies
ESTIC-2026, the second edition of India’s Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave, will be held from 27–29 October 2026.The event will be held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, under the theme
“Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science, Empowering Technologies.”
Organised by the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR), ESTIC-2026 will advance emerging science and technology frontiers. These include
Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and other emerging technologies with potential for transformative applications. The conclave will catalyse strategic collaborations and support India’s vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.Spanning 12 thematic areas, the event will feature plenary sessions, technical discussions and exhibitions.
Read More on Agenda:
ESTIC 2026
Understanding Additive Manufacturing Technology
AM is not just another manufacturing tool - it is a form of digital engineering that brings in a digital file that completely controls the layer-by-layer material deposition and sometime material composition to build an object. It brings in convergence of computing, electronics, design software and materials science. Every AM object starts out as a
digital file
, so the technology is closely linked to tools like
Computer-Aided Design (CAD),
Artificial Intelligence and pattern recognition. AM works on a simple but powerful idea - building an object up, rather than cutting it down. Here is how a digital design turns into a physical object, step by step:
Virtual design
: The process begins with a digital design made in a CAD (Computer-Aided Design) file - either modelled from scratch or captured using a 3D scanner or now a days made using AI from mobile phone photos.
STL file:
A STL (Standard Tessellation Language) file represents a 3D model as a collection of triangular surfaces. It is one of the commonly used file formats for preparing models for AM. This file instructs what to build to the machine.
Slicing
: Slicing software divides this digital model into hundreds or thousands of horizontal layers. Once done it instructs machine how to print layer-by-layer.
Printing
: The sliced file is fed into the AM machine, which reads each layer and builds the object step by step.
Additive Process
: An AM object is built by laying down successive layers of material until it takes its final shape. Technology evolution has taken digital manufacturing to such accuracies in deposition and composition control that without the digital instructions printing process fails to build properly. Currently there are 40+ such processes in market and R&D stage.
Final object
: The printer fuses successive layers of material together into a single, complete three-dimensional object. Once printed, post processing is done to make it marketable.
Additive Manufacturing Materials
In myriad applications, the following material categories have been revolutionary in Additive Manufacturing.
Thermoplastics:
Thermoplastic polymers are the most popular types of AM materials. Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polycarbonate (PC) and polylactic acid (PLA) each offer distinct advantages in different applications. Water-soluble polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is typically used to create temporary support structures, which are later dissolved away.
Metals:
Different metals and metal alloys are used in additive manufacturing, which include precious metals like gold and silver to strategic metals like stainless steel and titanium.
Ceramics:
A variety of ceramics including zirconia, alumina and tricalcium phosphate are also used in additive manufacturing. Also, alternate layers of powdered glass and adhesive are baked together to develop entirely new classes of glass products.
Bio Materials:
The biomaterials used in AM applications include the hardened material like silicon, calcium phosphate and zinc to support bone structures as new bone growth occurs. The bio-inks fabricated from stem cells are also being explored by researchers to form blood vessels, bladders and many other human organs. Also 3D Printing of human organs such as liver tissues, kidney, heart etc. are being printed using biomaterials and living cells.
Reshaping Key Sectors of the Indian Economy
AM is no longer confined to labs and prototypes. It is already being adopted across critical sectors of India's economy and Strategic Sector, backed by government and private players projects on the ground.
Space & Aerospace
India's space programme is embracing additive manufacturing to build lighter, faster hardware. In May 2024, IIT Madras-incubated start-up
Agnikul Cosmos
launched
Agnibaan - SOrTeD
, featuring a
single-piece, AM printed semi-cryogenic rocket engine
. The mission demonstrated how additive manufacturing can enable complex engine designs and support faster, indigenous development of space hardware. NSAM is helping more such start-ups in their R&D for development of critical engine parts using AM.
Defence
The Armed Forces are turning to AM for faster, disaster-resilient construction. The Indian Army inaugurated its first AM-printed two-story dwelling unit at Ahmedabad, built in just 12 weeks, and has since extended the technology to precast defenses in operational terrains like Ladakh. NSAM is supporting all three branches of defense for establishing workshop level facilities for MRO applications.
Healthcare
India is building indigenous alternatives to imported medical technology through AM. MeitY has supported AM based medical device manufacturing and startups like OsteoForge that is AM printing natural silk-based implant development under NSAM. The Technology Development Board is supporting 3D-printed bone grafts made from indigenous bioceramic materials. The technology can create grafts customised to a patient’s specific needs and anatomy. It can reduce imports, strengthen domestic medical manufacturing and support more personalised healthcare.
Electronics
India's network of AM centres is building indigenous capability in electronics-grade manufacturing. NSAM has successfully demonstrated AM printed electronics components such as batteries, antennas, varistors, capacitors and many more.  A globally first, IISc has demonstrated Photonic Integrated Circuit blocks using AM printing.
Construction
India is exploring 3D printing as a potential solution for faster and more sustainable construction. The Kelvin 6K Pro, an on-site 3D construction printer, has demonstrated the ability to build 2,500 sq ft homes in under 30 days using low-carbon geopolymer material. The technology has the potential to reduce material and logistics costs, lower carbon emissions and improve construction efficiency. Early applications indicate potential for 30% lower material and logistics costs and 90% lower emissions compared with cement-based construction.
Behind this growing momentum lies a clear government push. Over the past few years, the Centre has moved from isolated pilot projects to a structured, mission-mode approach for Additive Manufacturing -backed by dedicated funding, institutions and a national strategy. NSAM is now developing concrete based supercapacitors for solar energy storage.
Government Policy Initiatives: Building an Indian AM Ecosystem
Recognizing AM as a strategic, next-generation manufacturing technology, the Government of India is building a structured national ecosystem. This effort is anchored in the National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM). It is supported by growing national platforms, institutions and initiatives that are strengthening the ecosystem.
National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM)
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) released the National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM) in February 2022. NSAM serves as India’s guiding policy framework for 3D printing and additive manufacturing. Aligned with
Make in India
and
Atmanirbhar Bharat
, the strategy sets clear, time-bound national targets. These targets are being pursued through collaboration among the Centre, States, industry and academia.
The national strategy
aims
to
capture
5% of the global additive manufacturing market
and add nearly
US$1 billion to India’s GDP
. It also targets the development of
50 India-specific additive manufacturing technologies
, covering materials, machines, processes and software.
The strategy also seeks to nurture
100 new additive manufacturing start-ups
and develop
500 new products
. It also aims to train
1 lakh skilled workers
for the additive manufacturing workforce. Another objective is to build additive manufacturing capabilities across
10 existing and emerging manufacturing sectors
.
To further advance these objectives, the Government has established
seven specialised Development and Deployment Centres
. These centres support research and development, skilling and hands-on technology access.
Did you Know?
The Government of India is nurturing 3D printing skills at the school level through
Atal Tinkering Labs (ATLs).
Each lab receives a grant of ₹20 lakh to set up dedicated innovation workspaces of 1,200–1,500 sq ft, equipped with Do-it-Yourself (DIY) kits including 3D printers, Robotics, and Internet of Things (IoT). This gives students from Grade VI to Grade XII hands-on exposure to Additive Manufacturing early on - helping build India's future AM workforce from the classroom itself.
Progress Under NSAM
More than four years after its launch, the
National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM)
has made steady and measurable progress. Government-supported initiatives have strengthened India’s additive manufacturing ecosystem through skilling, entrepreneurship, technology development and sectoral applications.
More than
1,54, 000 individuals
have been trained in additive manufacturing-related skills, creating a growing skilled workforce.
Fifty-six additive manufacturing start-ups
have also been supported, strengthening India’s innovation and entrepreneurship base. The network of national centres has enabled the development of
65
India-specific technologies including materials, machines, Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM) and printed products
. These capabilities are supporting the development of products and prototypes across
aerospace, medical devices, electronics, energy, food processing and photonics
.
NSAM 2.0
NSAM 2.0 is being conceptualised to support India’s aspiration for AM market acceleration. The next phase plans to accelerate Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) generation, grow AM network through Digital Integration and proposes to develop globally competitive additive manufacturing technologies for commercialization. It aims to improve the affordability of machines and materials through clusters and strengthen the additive manufacturing electronics value chain.
NSAM 2.0 is planning to expand the additive manufacturing start-up base, provide extensive support to Indian defense and promote Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)-driven pilot programmes. It proposes to deepen international cooperation through standards, joint research and technology partnerships. These priorities can strengthen India’s technological capabilities and mainstream additive manufacturing across economic, industrial and societal applications.
National Additive Manufacturing Symposium (NAMS)
NAMS is a national platform for advancing India’s Additive Manufacturing (AM) ecosystem. It brings policymakers, scientists, industry, start-ups, academia and other AM stake holders together on a common platform. The platform promotes coordinated progress across policy, research, innovation and industry.
MeitY organised the 2nd NAMS edition on 13 March 2026 in New Delhi. NAMS 2026 strengthened collaboration across India’s AM ecosystem. MoUs were exchanged to deepen ecosystem partnerships, alongside the launch of new AM products. Panel discussions covered NSAM 2.0, defence adoption, industry perspectives and MeitY-supported R&D centres. The symposium also strengthened inter-ministerial coordination on AM applications. State Governments, industry and leading research institutions further strengthened the platform. These efforts highlight the growing relevance of AM across diverse sectors of the Indian economy.
Towards a Viksit Bharat
AM is steadily moving from India’s research labs into factories, defence establishments and hospitals. Backed by focused government policies, it is strengthening indigenous manufacturing and reducing reliance on imports. It is also supporting the vision of
Atmanirbhar Bharat
through greater domestic technological capabilities. As India scales its Additive Manufacturing ecosystem, it is creating skilled employment and strengthening its technology base. The technology also supports
Industry 5.0
through digital production, advanced automation, distributed and flexible manufacturing. Its applications can further contribute to
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
through resource efficiency, localised production and sustainable solutions. Together, these efforts position AM as an emerging contributor to India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat.

title: CCI approves proposed combination related to internal restructuring of the JSW Group
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                07 OCT 2026 8:00PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has approved the proposed combination related to internal restructuring of the JSW Group.
The parties to the combination are JSW Steel Limited (JSW Steel), JSW Projects Limited (JSW Projects), and BMM Ispat Limited (BMM).
The Proposed Combination is an internal group restructuring within the JSW Group with the objective of consolidating JSW Group’s majority interest in BMM into full ownership. Currently, JSW Group (through JSW Projects) holds 58.47% equity shareholding in BMM, and BMM is commercially integrated within JSW Group’s supply chain through intra-group sales and procurements. With the intent to enhance operational, financial, and organisational efficiencies through economies of scale, resource pooling, and rationalisation of capital, JSW Group proposes to fully absorb BMM by way of an amalgamation into JSW Steel.
JSW Steel, listed on the National Stock Exchange of India Limited and BSE Limited, is primarily engaged in the manufacture and sale of a diverse range of iron and steel products in India and abroad and forms part of the JSW Group. With fully integrated operations spanning across mining, raw material processing, steel production and downstream value-added manufacturing.
JSW Projects is an unlisted public limited company headquartered at Mumbai, and forms part of the JSW Group. JSW Projects is engaged in the business of manufacturing iron ore pellets, Sponge Iron / DRI, and power generation for captive use, which are ultimately used in the manufacture of steel and steel products only for JSW Steel.
BMM, a public limited company incorporated in India, is a steel manufacturing company engaged in producing semi-finished and long steel products and operates an approximately 1 MTPA integrated steel manufacturing facility in Karnataka.
As an integrated facility, BMM undertakes the full steelmaking process, from ironmaking through to finished long-product rolling, within its Karnataka plant.
